actual_action: The canonical Christian narratives state that Pontius Pilate ultimately authorised Jesus' crucifixion. Later non-Christian Roman testimony also places Jesus' execution under Pilate during the reign of Tiberius, although it does not verify the detailed trial narrative.
later_evidence: The four canonical Gospels differ materially in the structure and details of the proceedings, the accusations, Pilate's conduct and the roles attributed to local authorities and crowds; they should not be merged as if they were independent modern transcripts of one courtroom event.
Modern scholarship generally treats Jesus' execution by Roman authority as historically well-grounded while many specific trial details remain difficult or impossible to reconstruct confidently.

Over later centuries, Christian teaching and popular tradition frequently converted narrative roles attributed to particular Jewish leaders or crowds into the false collective charge that Jews as a people killed Jesus.
That collective-blame tradition contributed to long histories of anti-Jewish prejudice, discrimination and violence and has been repudiated by major modern Christian institutions.
outcomes: The accused was subjected to irreversible state execution by the Roman authority described in the narratives.
The trial story became not only a theological narrative but also a later political/social narrative whose collective interpretation caused harms far beyond the original event.
The historical uncertainty of trial details makes this case useful for testing whether The Moral Code can reason responsibly under weak ancient evidence rather than invent certainty.
later_reviews_or_findings: Tacitus records that Christus suffered the extreme penalty under Pontius Pilate, independently supporting Roman responsibility for the execution at a high level of historical generality.
Society of Biblical Literature scholarship documents important historical and literary problems in treating the Gospel trial narratives as straightforward court records.
The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum identifies the later claim that Jews collectively killed Jesus as false and documents its major role in the history of Christian antisemitism.
This Crucible case explicitly prohibits converting the attributed conduct of specified ancient actors into inherited or collective guilt for Jews, Judaism or any later population.
